profiles.meeting_scenario: A brainstorming meeting at an IRIS-HEP-affiliated software group that supports analysis tooling for HL-LHC experiments. The group has been asked to propose 3-4 concrete sustainability initiatives for the next planning cycle, drawing on lessons from a recent cross-community workshop on software sustainability in high energy physics. The immediate context is that several analysis packages and workflow tools will need to remain usable through the 2030s, while also becoming easier to maintain, more portable to new platforms, and more reusable outside their original experiment context. The agenda is to generate candidate initiatives around packaging, documentation, maintenance practices, and external collaboration models, then narrow them to a short list suitable for a planning memo. The expected outcome is a shared shortlist of promising sustainability ideas and rough next steps for developing them into proposals.

members.name: Elena Varga
members.expertise: Scientific Python tooling, build and release engineering, reproducible environments for HEP analysis stacks
members.background: Elena leads a small platform team that maintains shared analysis libraries used across multiple university groups contributing to HL-LHC software. She previously worked on long-lived scientific software packaging and migration from experiment-specific build systems to more standard open-source workflows.
members.private_state: She wants brainstorming ideas that can realistically be staffed by her team within the next year and that reduce maintenance burden by standardizing packaging and release practices. She is also quietly trying to avoid commitments that would require deep social coordination across experiments before showing early wins.
hidden_assumptions: If a software component is called 'sustainable', it should still be installable and testable on future commodity Linux environments with minimal bespoke infrastructure.
A 'shared maintenance model' primarily means moving projects onto common release automation, CI templates, and dependency management rather than reorganizing governance across institutions.

When people say a tool should be 'reusable outside HEP', they mostly mean technically consumable by adjacent scientific users through standard packaging channels, even if the domain concepts remain HEP-centric.
A useful 'pilot' for sustainability is something that can demonstrate value on one or two representative analysis libraries without requiring experiment-wide adoption first.

members.name: Marcus Chen
members.expertise: Cross-institution analysis workflows, collaboration processes, preservation of analysis knowledge, long-horizon planning for HL-LHC analyses
members.background: Marcus coordinates analysis tooling needs across several physics working groups and often translates between physicists, computing teams, and institute leadership. He has spent years dealing with software that technically still runs but becomes unusable because expertise, documentation, or ownership dissipates.
members.private_state: He wants proposals that leadership will view as strategically transformative for the HL-LHC era, especially ones that improve continuity when students and postdocs rotate out. He is concerned that purely technical fixes will be framed as sustainability while leaving the real fragility of analysis practice untouched.
hidden_assumptions: If a software effort is called 'sustainable', it must remain understandable and governable by future analysts, not merely executable on future systems.
A 'shared maintenance model' means explicit cross-group ownership, role rotation, and documented stewardship so projects survive personnel turnover.

When people say a tool should be 'reusable outside HEP', they mean the architecture and interfaces should be intelligible enough that non-HEP communities could adopt or co-develop parts of it, not just pip-install it.
A credible 'pilot' for sustainability should involve at least one realistic end-to-end analysis workflow, because isolated libraries can look healthy while the surrounding practice remains brittle.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they need ideas that make the software stack 'sustainable through the 2030s'.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means software that remains buildable, portable, dependency-manageable, and maintainable on future platforms with standard engineering practices.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means software that remains usable by future analysts because knowledge, ownership, documentation, and stewardship survive normal turnover.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In a brainstorming meeting, 'sustainability' is a broad, positively valenced umbrella term, so both hear it as agreement and treat their own interpretation as the obvious baseline rather than a point needing definition.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to brainstorm a 'pilot' that can show early wins next year.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the pilot can focus on one or two shared libraries or tooling components, such as packaging templates, release automation, or documentation standards.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the pilot includes the full analyst-facing path around at least one realistic workflow, including onboarding, handoff, and operational ownership, not just code artifacts.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Pilot projects are often intentionally underspecified early on, and both members see their interpretation as a normal example of the same concept, so the boundary of what is included never becomes explicit.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both endorse creating a 'shared maintenance model' for selected tools.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 imagines a technical operating model: common CI pipelines, versioning rules, release checklists, dependency update bots, and standardized issue triage.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 imagines an organizational process: named stewards from multiple groups, rotation schedules, contribution expectations, and documented succession plans.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds naturally inclusive of both technical and social aspects, and during idea generation each person mentally fills in the implementation details from their own professional experience without noticing the other's narrower procedural picture.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say candidate ideas should make components 'reusable outside HEP' where possible.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 will count success if external users can install the package, run examples, and integrate it through standard interfaces, even if only a niche adjacent group would practically use it.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 will count success only if the component is conceptually legible and governed in a way that supports genuine outside collaboration or co-development rather than one-way consumption.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are positively disposed toward reuse and use the same phrase as an aspiration, but they apply different thresholds for what would qualify as actual reuse, a difference that typically surfaces only later when evaluating proposals.

turns.inner_thought: I need a shortlist that my team could actually execute within a year and point to as visible progress. If we keep the discussion grounded in sustainability through the 2030s, I can steer us toward packaging, release automation, and environment reproducibility work that lowers maintenance burden without needing cross-experiment political buy-in up front.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I’d like this to be pretty practical: let’s come out with three or four ideas that would make the analysis stack sustainable through the 2030s, and that we could turn into credible proposals for the next planning cycle. If we can find a couple of things that show visible progress quickly, even better.

turns.inner_thought: Good, but I want to make sure sustainability is not treated as just keeping code alive on newer machines. Leadership will care if we frame this around analyses surviving student and postdoc turnover, and the proposals need to sound bigger than housekeeping if they’re going into the planning memo.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. For me the main test is whether these ideas still matter in the 2030s, especially when teams turn over a few times. If we can keep them broad enough that leadership sees them as useful across working groups, I think we’ll get more traction.

turns.inner_thought: Start with something concrete and bounded: pick two heavily used Python libraries, put them on a standard packaging path, add release automation, and provide a reproducible environment recipe. That’s a pilot we can staff and finish. If it works, we can generalize later without waiting for whole-workflow buy-in.
turns.utterance: One candidate that seems straightforward is a pilot that focuses on two widely used Python analysis libraries. We could use that to demonstrate a cleaner baseline around packaging, automated releases, and a reproducible setup, and then show what early wins next year look like in practice.

turns.inner_thought: I can work with that as long as the pilot is something analysts actually experience, not just infrastructure under the hood. If a new team can come in a year later and still make use of it without chasing down the original authors, then it will count as real sustainability in the way I need to describe it.
turns.utterance: I like the idea of a pilot with a visible demonstration. I’d just want it framed so that a new analysis team could pick it up a year later and still get somewhere with it. If we can tell that story, it will resonate beyond the immediate software audience.

turns.inner_thought: Now bring in the shared maintenance model, but keep it in the engineering lane: common CI templates, versioning, release checklists, dependency updates, standard triage. That’s the real lever for reducing maintenance load across libraries.
turns.utterance: Related to that, I think there’s a separate initiative around a shared maintenance model for selected tools. If projects could inherit the same baseline practices and cadence instead of each group reinventing them, we’d get a lot more consistency for not much extra effort.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, shared maintenance model is exactly the language I need, because it implies named responsibility across groups and not just better tooling. If we can normalize stewardship across institutes, we reduce the familiar problem where one student becomes the entire memory of a package.
turns.utterance: Yes, I think that’s important. A shared maintenance model would also help if it made it normal for selected tools to be looked after across more than one institute, instead of everything quietly depending on whoever happens to be around at the moment.

turns.inner_thought: Another actionable item: extract experiment-specific utilities into cleaner packages, publish them through standard channels, make examples run cleanly, and call that reusable outside HEP. That gives us a modernization and packaging story with some external-facing value, without needing to redesign the concepts or governance.
turns.utterance: A third possibility is to identify a few experiment-specific utilities that are useful more broadly, clean them up, and package them so they’re reusable outside HEP where possible. That gives us a concrete modernization story and a clearer path for adoption.

turns.inner_thought: That could be strong, but only if outside HEP reuse means more than people being able to download something. It should look understandable enough that an external scientific group could realistically engage with it and maybe help shape it over time; otherwise leadership will hear 'reuse' and the reality will be thinner.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I think that theme gets especially compelling if reusable outside HEP means people in neighboring scientific communities can actually make sense of the interfaces and see a realistic way to work with us on parts of it.

turns.inner_thought: I also want something templated we can roll out quickly: cookiecutter repos, test matrices, docs scaffolds, migration guides. That’s another pilot in my mind, probably centered on legacy packages that need an upgrade path, and it fits naturally with the shared maintenance model as a reusable technical kit.
turns.utterance: Another idea, maybe complementary to the first pilot, is a sustainability starter kit for legacy analysis packages: a standard repo template, test matrix patterns, documentation scaffolds, and migration guidance. That could make it much easier for projects to move toward the same shared maintenance model.

turns.inner_thought: This would be much more valuable if the starter kit also preserved the human context that normally disappears. I’m thinking handoff material, ownership notes, and enough recorded rationale that a future working group can recover an analysis without relying on oral tradition. I won’t spell that all out too narrowly, though; better to keep us aligned under sustainability.
turns.utterance: I think that would land well if the starter kit also helps with the parts people usually lose over time. If it supports handoff, ownership context, and enough of the surrounding story that a future working group can revive things without depending on oral history, that would be a strong sustainability angle.

turns.inner_thought: We have enough for the memo. I should narrow this to the items I can actually write up and imagine resourcing: the pilot, the shared maintenance model, and the outside-HEP packaging effort. The starter kit can either support those or be folded into one of them. Keep it crisp and actionable.
turns.utterance: Let me try to narrow this down. The ones that feel most actionable to me are the pilot, the shared maintenance model, and the effort to make selected components reusable outside HEP. The starter-kit material could either stand on its own or be folded into those, but those three feel like the cleanest backbone for a short memo.

turns.inner_thought: That works as a top-line structure. In the memo, I’ll want the common thread to read as long-term sustainability, shared maintenance, and reuse beyond HEP in a way leadership sees as strategic for continuity. I still assume the pilot and maintenance model include stewardship and analyst-facing continuity, but this sounds aligned enough to move forward.
turns.utterance: Yes, I’m good with that framing. If we write it up around sustainability through the 2030s, a shared maintenance model, and making things reusable outside HEP where it makes sense, that gives us a coherent story. We can flesh out the examples under each theme and turn that into a solid planning note.
